paras: The steamer Dacotah killings were an attack on Black deckhands aboard the Ohio River steamer Dacotah, laid up near Catlettsburg, Kentucky, in late November 1880, in which the second mate and four white crewmen killed two Black men and seriously wounded two others. The rest of the boat's twenty-two Black deckhands were driven off the boat, and the story ran in white newspapers from Maine to Nebraska as a "bloody riot."

According to a passenger who reached Wheeling on the steamer Buckeye State, the Dacotah was bound for Huntington deeply laden when low water forced her to the bank five miles below Catlettsburg. Her deck crew was made up of twenty-two Black men and four white men, not counting the officers, and there had been trouble between the mate and the Black deckhands. Once the boat laid up, the crew was paid off and the Black men were given transportation tickets to Cairo.

The Washington Evening Star placed the violence on "Sunday last," which would be November 28. In every version, the Black crewmen attacked the mate before leaving, and the second mate and the four white men went to his assistance. In the fight that followed, two Black men were shot and seriously wounded and two were killed with a monkey wrench and an axe, after which the remaining Black crewmen were driven from the boat. The Wheeling informant could learn only one name, that of the second mate, John Craft, who was "reported" to have done the shooting.
None of the reports names the dead or wounded, and no report of an arrest, inquest or prosecution was found in the coverage.

All the coverage came from the white press and traced to the steamer Buckeye State, whose report went out in wire dispatches datelined Cincinnati and Cleveland. The Portland Daily Press and the Daily Kennebec Journal in Maine printed the Cincinnati wire on November 30 under "BLOODY RIOT" and "Bloody Riot on a Steamer." The Omaha Daily Bee ran a Cleveland version the same day and advertised it on its front page as a "Bloody Fight With Darkies on an Ohio River Steamer."

Closer to the scene, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer headed its fuller passenger account "RIOTOUS ROUSTABOUTS," casting the Black deckhands as the rioters even as it named a white officer as the man who fired. Each version accepted that the Black crew had started the fight, and none carried an account from the Black deckhands themselves. The Evening Star's short paragraph of December 3 called it "a bloody affray" and said the surviving Black men were "driven ashore."
The Cleveland dispatch printed in Omaha said the two men were killed with a monkey wrench, while the Cincinnati wire, the Wheeling account and the Evening Star named both a monkey wrench and an axe.

accounts.label: Buckeye State wire report
accounts.gist: The Black crew, after being paid off, attacked the mate; the second mate and four white men came to his aid, and in the fight two Black men were shot, two killed and the rest driven off.

accounts.label: Buckeye State passenger at Wheeling
accounts.gist: Same sequence, adding that the boat was bound for Huntington, the Black crew had been given tickets to Cairo, and second mate John Craft reportedly did the shooting.

accounts.label: Washington Evening Star paragraph
accounts.gist: A rewritten version dating the 'bloody affray' to Sunday and saying the remaining Black crewmen were 'driven ashore.'

framing.detail: The Portland Daily Press and the Kennebec Journal ran the Cincinnati wire under 'BLOODY RIOT' with the subhead 'Two Negroes Killed and Two Seriously Wounded.'
The Wheeling Intelligencer headed its passenger's account 'RIOTOUS ROUSTABOUTS,' casting the Black deckhands as the rioters, but named the second mate as the reported shooter.
The Omaha Bee listed the item in its front-page deck as a 'Bloody Fight With Darkies on an Ohio River Steamer.'

conflicts.note: The Cleveland version omits the axe; most versions name both.
The Wheeling passenger account is the most specific and closest to the source.
